title: Ashoka's words
tomorrow: why would a monk walk from China to India?

cards: An apology typed in a notes app, screenshotted, posted, then quietly deleted a week later. Words that can be taken back. A king in ancient India did the opposite.

He had won a war. And he had his regret about it carved into rock, where anyone passing could read it, and some of those rocks still stand. A gentle note for younger listeners: this text counts the dead of a war.

teach.b: The edict speaks in the king's own voice. He calls himself the Beloved of the Gods; history knows him as Ashoka. Eight years after he became king, he says, he conquered Kalinga.
A hundred and fifty thousand people were carried off, a hundred thousand were killed, and many times that number died. Then the turn.
After that, he says, came an intense devotion to dhamma, and remorse. He names what grieves him: when a free land is conquered, there's killing, death and people dragged from home.
And it falls hardest on the decent people living there, kind to their parents, teachers and friends, who lose the ones they love. Even a small part of that suffering, he says, would weigh on him now.

teach.h: A NEW VICTORY: CONQUEST BY DHAMMA.
teach.b: So he names a new victory: conquest by dhamma. And he says why he had it carved: so his sons and grandsons won't think a new conquest worth making. That's a Buddhist shape of remorse.

teach.h: SEE IT, AMEND IT, HOLD BACK.
teach.b: The Buddha once described it to another king, one with his own father's blood on his hands: to see a wrong as a wrong, make amends, and hold back from then on, that is growth.
Not endless guilt. Not a quiet hope that everyone forgets. A wrong, named where it can't be deleted, and a new rule after it.

how: Ashoka's edicts are read by Buddhists and historians alike, and Buddhist teachers point to the thirteenth as a picture of remorse that changes conduct; in Buddhist practice, confession means seeing a wrong as a wrong, making amends and resolving restraint.

o: a book of laws a pilgrim copied out in India
a monk's verses about a battle among the gods
a king's rock-carved words, with his remorse for a war

games.q: inside the edict — tap the pairs.

s: the edict hides the war's cost to make the king look good
it counts the captured, the killed and the dead, and names his own remorse.
the king says he had it carved so his descendants wouldn't seek new conquests
so his sons and grandsons won't think a new conquest worth making.
the edict ends in guilt alone, with nothing changed
it names a new victory: conquest by dhamma.

games.q: a joke you posted about a classmate spread much further than you meant. what does the edict's kind of remorse look like?
o: own it where it spread, say it was wrong, and change what you post
delete it quietly and hope nobody remembers it was yours
post again and again about how terrible you feel
games.why: the king named his wrong in public stone and set a new rule after it: see a wrong as a wrong, make amends, hold back from then on.

practice: Press your palm flat on something hard and cool: a table, a wall, a stone if you have one. Let one small regret come to mind, and say silently what happened, plainly, as if you were carving it.
Then lift your hand and rest it in your lap: named, and set down.

wordCard.voice: Ashoka's words: the edicts a king had carved on rock and pillar, and in the thirteenth, his remorse for the Kalinga war.

orig.note: Pali and Prakrit: teaching, right conduct; the king's word for the way he chose.

carryVoice: Here's the line: carved remorse, a wrong named where it can't be deleted, with a new rule after it. Stone set.
